1.pericope_label: Alleluia: the heavenly hosts praise God for judging the great whore

schools.summary: Give the Hebrew behind the acclamation and trace it into pagan hymnody; follow the divine name from “I will be” to “he that is”, the future swallowed up in a present where the coming is no longer awaited; restrict the elders to the Church gathered from the Jews; explain the order in which the two heavenly companies are named by the direction in which praise is moving; and and press the conclusion that the reversal marks the fulfilment of the judgments.

Count the occurrences of the acclamation and locate the Hallel; lay the chapter out as an episode delaying the catastrophe; distinguish the elders as representatives of the Church from the living beings as representatives of nature and correct the tense of the participle; render the smoke as continuing to rise; and render the smoke as continuing to rise.

Reduce the harlot’s guilt to corrupting the bad and persecuting the good, and take those two as comprehending all the crimes of the wicked; insist that the text says the smoke rises and not that it will rise, Babylon being already in part on fire; and explain that the Hebrew words are left untranslated out of reverence for their sacredness.
Take the elders and living creatures for the churches and their ministers through the successive periods, and read the repeated acclamation as a mark of how hearty and constant the praise was.

Attend to what the praise accomplishes rather than what it asserts — prayers turned into praises, hosannas ending in halleluias, and the fire burning the fiercer for the shout — and draw the rule that thanking God for what is done is the most effectual way of praying for what is not.

debates: Who the four and twenty elders represent — the churches of every period (Gill), the Church as against the living creatures who represent nature (Ellicott), or specifically the Church gathered out of the Jews (Clarke).
Whether the smoke rising is present or future, which Bede rests on the tense and Robertson on the aspect of the verb.
Why the elders are named before the living creatures here when the order is reversed elsewhere, a question only Wesley raises and answers.
outliers: Wesley alone explains the reversed order of the heavenly companies by the direction in which praise travels.
Bede alone gives a reason for leaving the Hebrew acclamation untranslated.
Clarke alone traces the form of the acclamation into pagan hymns to Apollo.
Henry alone treats the praise as itself an instrument, making the fire burn fiercer and the deliverance more complete.

5.pericope_label: The voice from the throne, the multitude like many waters, and the marriage of the Lamb

schools.summary: Exclude God and the Lamb as the source of the voice; distinguish the indistinct roar of this multitude from the articulate shout of the first, on grounds of both sound and grammar, and identify it with the redeemed rather than the angels; make the verb of reigning ingressive; and on the linen take the plural “righteousnesses”, holding that the robe is given and yet genuinely the wearer’s, with work left for the Bride as well as for Christ.

Report the variant that adds “our” to the title of God, and take comfort in an Almighty who never lets go the reins; expect from the marriage a state of Christianity more glorious than any before, and one near at hand though its content is unknown even to the spirits of the just; and deny outright that the fine linen is imputed righteousness, since the text calls it the righteousness of the saints wrought in them by the Spirit.

Describe the heavenly chorus as music without discord or an untuned key; prefer the conversion of the Jews to the general resurrection as the occasion; and take the bride’s robe for Christ’s righteousness both imputed for justification and imparted for sanctification.
Explain the material of the bridal dress itself, the byssus that was brought out of Judea into Egypt and used there in most holy things.

debates: Whose the voice from the throne is — a responsive company nearest the throne (Barnes), an angel of the Presence (Robertson), or the four living creatures (Wesley), all agreeing it cannot be God, since it says “our God”.

What the fine linen is: imputed righteousness received by faith (Barnes), expressly not imputed but wrought in the saints by the Spirit (Clarke), or both at once (Henry, Wesley), with Ellicott and Robertson taking it as real righteousness that is nonetheless a gift.
When the marriage occurs — at the conversion of the Jews, at the general resurrection, in a coming age of the Church, or speedily and in a manner not yet known.
Why the second multitude sounds indistinct where the first was clear, which Barnes explains by distance and Robertson by the inarticulacy of waters and thunder.
outliers: Barnes alone distinguishes the two acclamations by the clarity of the sound, and alone quotes a pagan poet for the comparison.
Clarke alone rules imputation out of the verse, and alone reports the variant reading of the divine title.
Ellicott alone excludes the verse from the song and explains the dress as a deliberate answer to the harlot’s.
Gill alone describes the plant from which the linen was made.

9.pericope_label: Blessed are they called to the marriage supper; John falls at the angel’s feet and is refused

schools.summary: Leave the speaker unidentified between three candidates; and treat John’s prostration as a plain fault that cannot be excused or justified, worship being due to God alone.

Identify the speaker with the angel of the seventeenth chapter; count the beatitude among the benedictions of the book and warn against pressing the imagery — the bride and the guests are not to be sharply distinguished, and apocalyptic symbolism has laws of its own; fence the refusal so that it forbids homage to angels without touching the worship of Christ; and take the checking of the impulse as evidence for the book’s genuineness against pretended revelations.

Divide over the act itself — one voice holding that John mistook the angel for the angel of the covenant and that worship of any creature is flat idolatry, the other that he could not have made such a mistake and that the prostration was oriental courtesy rather than worship, his error being to think himself indebted to the angel; and read the angel’s reason as an argument that a preaching commission ranks with the gift of prophecy.

debates: Whether John’s act was religious worship at all — Gill and Wesley say it was and was culpable, Clarke denies it was worship and calls it the reverence due to a superior, Robertson leaves the motive open.
Whom John took the angel for: the angel of the covenant (Wesley), a being who represented God (Robertson), or nobody he could have confused with Christ (Clarke, expressly).
How many benedictions the book contains — six (Ellicott) or seven (Robertson).
What the refusal proves: that homage to an angel is wrong, and, Barnes insists, nothing at all about whether Christ may be worshipped.
outliers: Clarke alone denies that the prostration was worship, and alone locates John’s error in a sense of obligation rather than in adoration.
Ellicott alone argues from the angel’s refusal to the authenticity of the book, contrasting it with pretended revelations.
Ellicott alone warns against distinguishing the bride from the wedding guests.
Barnes alone guards the passage against being turned into an argument about the worship of Christ.

11.pericope_label: Heaven opened: the rider called Faithful and True, whose name is the Word of God

schools.summary: Distinguish this vision from the first seal, from the war with the dragon, and from the last judgment, and identify it with the battle of Armageddon; and offer three possibilities for the blood on the vesture, preferring the blood of enemies not yet killed, with a Roman general’s purple as the figure behind it.

Place the expedition immediately after the marriage, and read the white horse as the equity of the cause and the certainty of success; allow that the blood may be his own, by which he purchased his mediatorial power, or his enemies’; and say of the unknown name only that the Word was God.

Divide over whether this rider is the rider of the first seal — one taking it as the same hope renewed after long despair, the other insisting the riders are very different; deny that the unknown name is unreadable rather than unfathomable; note that the many diadems answer the diadems of the dragon and the beast; and settle the reading of the stained garment for “sprinkled” on the strength of the prophetic original, the blood being the enemies’ and prophetically anticipated.

Split the double name — faithful in performing his promises, true in executing his threatenings — and make the white horse the mount of a general in triumph against the meekness of the ass; take the unknown name for the ineffable name the Jews will not pronounce, whose true sound was lost at the captivity; and identify the prophetic figure behind the bloodstained garment with a Maccabean conqueror.

debates: Whether the rider here is the rider of the first seal — Ellicott treats the vision as renewed, Robertson says the riders are very different, and Gill separates the two visions by their periods.
What “a name that no man knew” means: a name whose import only he can fathom (Barnes, Wesley, Henry) or the ineffable name that cannot be pronounced at all (Clarke).
Whose blood is on the vesture — his own, the saints’, or his enemies’; and whether it is blood already shed or anticipated before the battle.
Whether the garment is “sprinkled” or “dipped”, which Robertson decides from the Greek versions of the prophet against a bolder reading he reports.
outliers: Gill alone rules out three other identifications of the vision before naming his own.
Clarke alone takes the unknown name for the unpronounceable tetragrammaton, and alone names Judas Maccabeus as the figure behind the prophetic original.
Robertson alone observes that the many diadems answer the diadems worn by the dragon and the beast.
Ellicott alone reads the reappearance of the white horse as the vindication of a hope that had turned to despair.

14.pericope_label: The armies of heaven, the sharp sword, the rod of iron, and the name King of kings

schools.summary: Exclude the angels from the heavenly armies on the ground that the linen is the righteousness of saints, which is not the righteousness of angels; take the sword for the word of God or the sentence given according to it, noting the versions that add “twoedged” here; and explain the inscribed name from the custom of weaving names into garments.

Exclude the angels, whether by the dress or by the incongruity of mounted angels, and observe that the accompanying hosts witness the triumph rather than share the killing; mark that the sword has changed its office since the opening vision, one voice arguing it from the dropped epithet; render the rule as shepherding with an iron staff; and set the inscription among ancient inscribed images, with the name possibly on the sword-hilt.

Include angels and saints together under Christ as Captain; keep the sword in its earlier sense as the word of the Gospel that confounds enemies and comforts friends; read the iron rod as the alternative to a golden sceptre and trace its historical strokes, including a conquest the writer condemns as detestable while holding it a righteous judgment; and gather the evidence of inscribed images of deities and princes.

Refer the rod of iron to the kingdom of the Romans rather than to Christ’s rule, and bring in the stone cut without hands to say what overthrows it; and reach the title King of kings by way of the apostolic charge to keep the faith unspotted until the appearing.

debates: Who compose the armies of heaven — saints only, on the argument from their linen (Gill, Ellicott) or from the incongruity of mounted angels (Barnes), or angels and saints together (Clarke), with Robertson citing the angelic warfare of the earlier chapter.
Whether the sword out of the mouth still means the word preached (Clarke) or has become an instrument of destruction (Barnes, Ellicott, who argues it from the omission of “two-edged”).
What the rod of iron is: the shepherd’s staff of Christ’s own rule (Ellicott, Robertson, Wesley) or the kingdom of the Romans (Cyril).
Whether the armies take part in the slaughter, which Barnes denies from the prophet’s “I have trodden the winepress alone”.
outliers: Cyril alone assigns the rod of iron to an earthly empire rather than to Christ.
Barnes alone denies the accompanying hosts any share in the killing.
Ellicott alone builds an argument on the epithet the verse does not repeat.
Wesley alone applies the iron rod to modern history, and alone condemns the instrument while defending the judgment.

17.pericope_label: The angel standing in the sun calls the birds to the supper of the great God

schools.summary: Rule out the angel of the vial, the archangel of the trumpet, the ministering spirits and Christ himself before identifying the figure with the Gospel ministry, whose standing in the sun marks how conspicuous its preachers will be and how clearly they will then see; and read the eating of kings’ flesh as the Christian princes taking possession of the defeated kingdoms.

Take the angel as one of many messengers and admire the economy of the sentence while declining to explain the position, or else explain it precisely as the place from which the birds of prey would see him; trace the summons to Ezekiel and call the scene a sacrificial feast for the vultures; and go through the ranks of the slain one by one, noting that armies mix freemen and slaves.

Read the position as sheer luminosity and note that a modern poet drew his angel of the sun from it; set a rabbinic tradition of a twelve-month feeding of beasts beside the prophet’s figure; and take the whole as measuring the vastness of a universal destruction.

debates: Who the angel standing in the sun is — an order of Gospel ministers (Gill) or simply another of the book’s many messengers (Barnes, Robertson, Clarke).
Why he stands in the sun: for grandeur only, the reason not being stated (Barnes), because that is where the birds of prey would see him (Robertson), or to mark his luminosity (Clarke).
Whether eating the flesh of kings is carnage or conquest — Gill alone reads it as the Christian princes succeeding to the defeated kingdoms, against the literal slaughter the others assume.
Whether this battle is the same as the one at Har-Magedon and the later battle of Gog and Magog, a question Robertson raises without settling.
outliers: Gill alone identifies the angel with the Gospel ministry, and alone reads the supper as a transfer of dominions.
Barnes alone comments on the literary economy of the verse, and alone declines to look for a reason for the angel’s position.
Clarke alone traces a modern poet’s angel to this verse, and alone supplies a rabbinic parallel with a term of years.
Barnes alone identifies the military ranks in the list and reaches for a modern army to illustrate the mixture of free and bond.

19.pericope_label: The beast and the kings gathered against the rider; the beast and false prophet taken alive

schools.summary: Rule out the devil and the pagan empire before identifying the beast with the antichristian civil powers, western chiefly but eastern too; and take the slain remnant for the remains of Papists, Pagans and Mahometans everywhere.

Read the assembled powers as Roman, Pagan and Mohammedan making common cause, or else as the imperial cult and its priesthood; find a propriety in the leaders being reserved for severer punishment than their followers; and take the killing by the sword as a word spoken, with the possibility that the effect is moral rather than physical.

Decode the three figures as the Latin empire, the popes and the papal clergy; divide over the word “alive”, one voice building on it a symmetry between two who went alive into heaven and two who go alive into hell, the other taking it as “in the zenith of their power”; and admire the description for narrating a victory without narrating a battle.
Refer the gathering against the Lord and his Anointed not to the last battle but to a present denial that God is the Father of Christ.

debates: What the beast is — the antichristian civil powers (Gill), the Papal power in alliance with pagan and Mohammedan (Barnes), the Latin empire with the popes as its image and the clergy as its prophet (Clarke), or the imperial cult and its priesthood (the view Robertson reports).
Whether “cast alive” is literal, so that two enter torment without dying (Wesley), or means discomfited at the height of their power (Clarke).
Why the leaders are taken and the followers killed, which Barnes explains by the greater guilt of those who stirred up the war.
Whether the slaughter by the sword of the mouth is physical or moral, Barnes suggesting the powers are subdued by the word rather than destroyed.
outliers: Wesley alone builds the parallel of two taken alive into heaven and two into hell, and alone praises the chapter for describing a victory with no battle in it.
Clarke alone assigns a separate referent to each of the beast, the image and the false prophet.
Cyril alone applies the gathering to a contemporary denial rather than to a future battle.
Barnes alone suggests that the destruction of these powers may be a moral effect rather than a slaughter.
